claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets arise from differences in local chemical inhomogeneity.
Local chemical inhomogeneities modify solute–dislocation interactions.
Local chemical inhomogeneities modify the local stacking-fault-energy landscape.
Selective removal or adjustment of particular elements changes local defect structures and thereby alters activation of twinning and cross-slip.
Equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni can form a single-phase FCC alloy.
The relevant equiatomic quaternary and ternary derivatives can be prepared as comparable single-phase FCC alloys under identical thermomechanical processing.
Removing or reducing one or two constituents changes the local solute distribution.
Changes in local solute distribution change the strength of solute–dislocation interactions.
Stacking-fault energy influences whether deformation proceeds through ordinary dislocation slip, twinning, or transformation-mediated plasticity.
The cited evidence supports cross-slip as a composition-controlled deformation mode in this alloy family.
The balance among slip, cross-slip, and twinning determines strength, ductility, and failure behavior relative to the quinary alloy.
Alloys retaining critical solute concentrations that lower stacking-fault energy and promote twinning will have strength, strain hardening, and ductility similar to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Reducing the content of the key elements will increase effective stacking-fault energy.
An increase in effective stacking-fault energy will suppress mechanical twinning.
Suppression of twinning can reduce ductility or work-hardening capacity.
Dislocation slip and mechanical twinning are the primary plasticity mechanisms within the proposed scope.
Using identical thermomechanical processing allows mechanical differences to be attributed predominantly to local chemistry rather than gross microstructural differences.
The ternary CrCoNi alloy can outperform the equiatomic quinary alloy in cryogenic strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.
